D007-D015_h001.question:
I’ve been a bankruptcy lawyer for over twenty years—used to take pride in being sharp, in control, in winning tough cases. But for the past seven months, it’s like I’m underwater. I wake up every morning at 3 a.m., wide awake but completely drained, and just lie there, staring at the ceiling. Getting out of bed takes all my strength. I move so slowly, even tying my shoes feels exhausting.

Nothing feels real anymore. The win I got last month on a big case? Meant nothing. My emotions are just... dead. I’ve started seeing things—figures in the corner of meeting rooms, people who aren’t there. I know it sounds crazy, but I can’t shake the feeling my colleagues are sending me secret messages through case files, even the way they shuffle papers. I’ll catch myself jumping from one thought to something totally unrelated in court, losing my train mid-sentence.

I’ve had these hallucinations and paranoid thoughts for about six months now, but they’ve only ever come during this deep fog of depression. When I feel slightly better, they disappear. They don’t linger on their own—just ride with the lows.
D007-D015_h001.options:
A. Persistent Depressive Disorder
    B. Adjustment Disorder
    C. Major Depressive Disorder with Psychotic Features
    D. Schizoaffective Disorder (Depressive Type)
D007-D015_h001.answer: C. Major Depressive Disorder with Psychotic Features

D007-D015_h002.question:
I’ve been feeling down for over half a year—low, tired, just not myself. Since my husband passed, I can’t seem to get back into anything. I used to enjoy my knitting circles and church group, but now I don’t even want to get dressed. Falling asleep takes me two or three hours, even when I’m exhausted. I speak slower now, I know—I catch myself, but my thoughts feel heavy, like wading through mud.

But there’s more… things I can’t explain. For months, I’ve been sure my late husband was unfaithful, even though he’s gone. I see him sometimes, standing at the foot of the bed, or walking through the kitchen. I know that sounds impossible, but I see him as clearly as I see you. I’ve also seen strangers in the house—shadowy people who vanish when I get closer. I try to tell my daughter, but the words come out jumbled, like my mind disconnects. I’ll start to say something and lose track—she says it doesn’t make sense.

But here’s the thing—these thoughts and visions, they only happen when I’m feeling this deep sadness. I never had them before I became depressed. When I feel a little better, they fade. They only come with this darkness.
D007-D015_h002.options:
A. Persistent Depressive Disorder
    B. Adjustment Disorder
    C. Major Depressive Disorder with Psychotic Features
    D. Schizoaffective Disorder (Depressive Type)
D007-D015_h002.answer: C. Major Depressive Disorder with Psychotic Features

D007-D015_h003.question:
I’ve been feeling overwhelmingly sad for about seven months now—like a heaviness I can’t shake. I used to find joy in helping my clients, but now I just sit at my desk, barely able to write notes or even get up to refill my water. Some mornings, I wake up at 3 a.m., completely alert but stuck in bed, staring at the ceiling, too slow to move. It’s like my body won’t listen to my mind.

About six months ago, the strange thoughts started. I began to believe I was chosen to deliver a divine message—something about healing the world through empathy. I know it sounds far-fetched, but to me, it feels true. Sometimes, I smell burning rubber out of nowhere, even when there’s nothing around that could be burning. I mentioned it to my neighbor, and she said she smelled nothing.

But here’s what I need you to understand—I haven’t had these delusions or smells when I’m not depressed. They only come with the sadness, the exhaustion, the emptiness. When the depression lifts a little, they fade too. I can’t keep up with my caseload anymore—my speech gets jumbled, I lose my train of thought, jump from one idea to another. It’s affecting everything.
D007-D015_h003.options:
A. Persistent Depressive Disorder
    B. Adjustment Disorder
    C. Major Depressive Disorder with Psychotic Features
    D. Schizoaffective Disorder (Depressive Type)
D007-D015_h003.answer: C. Major Depressive Disorder with Psychotic Features

D007-D015_h004.question:
I’ve been feeling completely empty for almost nine months now—just dragging myself through auditions that go nowhere. I can’t even enjoy things I used to love, like filming or spending time with friends. It’s like joy doesn’t exist anymore. I’ve lost roles I knew I should’ve gotten, and my agent hasn’t called in months. Honestly, some days I barely speak because it takes me so long to form words. Sleep’s no escape either—night after night, I wake up screaming from these nightmares about being trapped on a stage with no audience, no exit.

But here’s the thing… I *know* it’s not all hopeless. The truth is, I’m not just any actor. I see things—visions of me receiving the Oscar, standing there while the whole world watches, and I *know* it’s real because I’ve seen it. Sometimes, I look in the mirror and see a glowing version of myself, like I’m already famous. I’ve told casting directors they’re in the presence of greatness, but I can’t always get the words out right—sometimes they stop understanding me halfway through.

I haven’t had a stable job in months, and I can’t even keep my thoughts straight when I’m depressed. But the visions and the certainty? They only come when I’m down, not before or after.
D007-D015_h004.options:
A. Persistent Depressive Disorder
    B. Adjustment Disorder
    C. Major Depressive Disorder with Psychotic Features
    D. Schizoaffective Disorder (Depressive Type)
D007-D015_h004.answer: C. Major Depressive Disorder with Psychotic Features

D007-D015_h005.question:
I’ve been feeling completely drained for about the last seven months, maybe a bit longer. As a documentary director, I’m used to long hours and stress, but now everything feels pointless. I can’t find joy in filming—something I used to love—and even meeting with close friends feels like a chore. I wake up around 3 a.m. every day, heart racing, and just stare at the ceiling. For the past six months, things got... stranger. I keep seeing shadowy figures in my apartment at night, like people standing in doorways, but when I turn on the light, no one’s there. I know it sounds crazy, but I genuinely believe the world is falling apart—like everything we know is collapsing into chaos and no one can see it but me. I call it "the unravelling." But here’s what I want you to know—this all started *after* the depression dug in. When I feel even slightly better, the shadows fade, and the thoughts about the end of everything don’t feel as real. I’ve never had these experiences when I wasn’t deeply down.
D007-D015_h005.options:
A. Persistent Depressive Disorder
    B. Adjustment Disorder
    C. Major Depressive Disorder with Psychotic Features
    D. Schizoaffective Disorder (Depressive Type)
D007-D015_h005.answer: C. Major Depressive Disorder with Psychotic Features

D007-D015_h006.question:

I stopped enjoying my weekends, stopped caring about the gardening I used to love. I’ve lost about fifteen pounds without even trying—just no appetite, no hunger, like my body forgot how to feel alive. It’s like there’s a deep emptiness inside me, like I’m just going through motions. I keep thinking about the one time I missed a critical audit three years ago—something small, but I replay it constantly, beating myself up.

They tell me I have a divine mission, that I’m destined to reveal financial secrets that’ll change the world. I know it sounds strange, but they feel so real. Sometimes I catch myself saying things that don’t make sense—my husband’s told me I’m hard to follow, like my words get tangled. But the strange thoughts and voices—they only come when I’m in this deep sadness. When I feel even slightly better, they fade completely. They’ve never been there without the depression.

A. Schizoaffective Disorder (Depressive Type)
    B. Major Depressive Disorder with Psychotic Features
    C. Persistent Depressive Disorder
    D. Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder

D007-D015_h007.question:
I’ve been feeling completely empty for over a year—like nothing matters because nothing is real anymore. As an ER nurse, I used to find purpose in saving lives, but now I’m convinced the world is ending, maybe already gone. I can feel it—everyone and everything is already dead, we’re just ghosts going through motions. Sometimes, I taste blood when I eat, even if it's just toast. It’s always metallic, like licking a battery. I told my coworker the other day that the “flurge is rising,” and she gave me that look—confused. I made up that word, but it makes sense to me: flurge is the rot inside everything, spreading.

I don’t eat much anymore—food tastes like ash, and I don’t deserve nourishment anyway. I replay every little mistake at work, like that time last year when I was two minutes late logging meds—what if that killed someone? I should’ve done better. The guilt eats at me. But here’s the thing—when I’ve felt even a little okay, the voices stop, the tastes disappear, the delusions fade. They only come back when the darkness returns. They don’t live without the depression.
D007-D015_h007.options:
A. Schizoaffective Disorder (Depressive Type)
    B. Major Depressive Disorder with Psychotic Features
    C. Persistent Depressive Disorder
    D. Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder

D007-D015_h008.question:

But here’s the thing—these thoughts and visions only come when I’m in this deep depression. When my mood lifts slightly, even briefly, the voices and meanings fade. They’ve never stuck around on their own. They only show up when I’m drowning in this sadness.

D007-D015_h009.question:

D007-D015_h010.question:

These thoughts and voices haven’t let up in over a year, but they only started when I became so low, and they’ve never left during this time. D007-D015_h011.question:

D007-D015_h012.question:

D007-D015_h013.question:

My husband says I’ve started mimicking his gestures, like a broken reflection.
